stem: Why is a thread called a lightweight process?

options.text: It has its own stack but shares the process's code and data

explanation: It has its own program counter, registers and stack.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: In which model can one blocking system call block the whole process?
explanation: All its user threads share one kernel thread.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: Threads of the same process share code, data and open files.
explanation: Each keeps its own program counter, registers and stack.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: Linux and Windows 95 to XP use which threading model?
explanation: Each user thread gets its own kernel thread.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: Which are benefits of multithreading listed in the book?
explanation: The fourth benefit is resource sharing.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: Which one is not a thread library named in the book?
explanation: The three are Pthreads, Win32 and Java threads.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: On a single-core chip, the threads of a multithreaded application are

options.text: Run one after the other only after each finishes

explanation: A multi-core chip allows true parallelism.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7

stem: In the many-to-many model, users are limited to one thread per process.
explanation: Users have no restriction on the number of threads.
source: CSC 321 DLC Final.pdf (Computer Operating System course book), Study Session 7
